title: A third of the evening's internet
teaches: Content delivery networks, caching at the edge, adaptive bitrate video, filling caches off-peak, and the cost of moving bytes

blocks.text: In June 2012 Netflix announced Open Connect, its own network for delivering video. Instead of paying other companies to carry its films, it would build servers packed with disks and give them, free, to internet providers to install inside their own networks, and put more at the exchange points where networks meet. Each server would hold the films its neighbourhood was likely to watch, so most of an evening's viewing would travel a few miles, from a rack in the provider's building to the homes it served.

The scale explains the decision. Within a few years Sandvine, a company that sells traffic-measuring equipment to providers, was reporting Netflix as about a third of all downstream internet traffic in North America at evening peak.[^sandvine] An HD stream runs at about 5 Mb/s. A million people watching at once is 5 Tb/s, and a large provider at 9 p.m. can have that many. One film of two hours at 5 Mb/s is 4.5 GB.

Netflix's builders had to **count the cost** in its plainest form: where bytes go and who pays to move them. An hour of video at 5 Mb/s is 2.25 GB. Suppose a hundred million hours are watched in a day, all sent from a cloud region at 2 cents a gigabyte. That is 225 petabytes and about $4.5 million a day, before any of it has crossed the long-distance links between the cloud and the viewer, which would have to be built for the evening peak and sit mostly idle at 4 a.m. The design question is how to send those bytes the shortest way, at the cheapest hour.

Netflix did not invent the idea. In 1998 Tom Leighton, a mathematician at MIT, and his graduate student Danny Lewin founded Akamai on the consistent hashing they had published the year before (lesson 5), to spread popular web content over thousands of caching servers placed in many networks.[^lewin] A **content delivery network** (CDN) is that: servers near the readers, each holding copies of popular content, with a way of sending each reader to a near one, usually by answering the reader's DNS lookup with a nearby server's address. The company whose content it is runs the **origin**, which holds everything. A CDN server that does not hold what is asked for fetches it from the origin and keeps a copy: **pull-through** caching, lesson 5's cache-aside run by the cache itself.

Moving bytes costs different amounts depending on whose wires they cross. Clouds charge for data leaving them by the gigabyte, a few cents each. A network that buys **transit**, the right to reach the rest of the internet through a bigger network, usually pays per megabit a second of its peak rate, measured at the 95th percentile of each month's five-minute samples.[^p95] Two networks that exchange roughly equal traffic often **peer**: connect directly and charge each other nothing. A server inside the provider's own network costs the provider rack space and power, and saves it transit, because the bytes never leave. Bytes are cheapest when they travel least.

An edge server cannot hold everything; a streaming catalogue, with every film at a dozen bitrates, runs to petabytes. It does not need to, because viewing is lopsided. Tonight's new series and last week's hit get a large share of all viewing, and the thousandth most popular film gets little. A common model, close to many real catalogues, is that the title at popularity rank *k* is watched in proportion to 1/*k*: the second title half as much as the first, the hundredth a hundredth as much, a **Zipf** distribution.

blocks.caption: A catalogue of 10,000 titles whose popularity falls off as 1/rank to a power s, and an edge cache holding the most popular. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Guess, then find the cache size that serves 90% of views with s at 1.0

blocks.text: Holding a tenth of the catalogue serves about three quarters of the viewing. Serving 90% takes well over a third of the catalogue, and the last few per cent need nearly all of it. Each doubling of the cache gains less than the one before: the **long tail** of titles that are each rarely watched but together add up to a lot. Steeper popularity, a larger *s*, makes a small cache better; flatter popularity makes every cache worse. So CDNs are built in **tiers**: small fast caches nearest the readers hold the head of the curve, larger ones further back (at exchange points, or in a region) hold more of the tail, and only the true rarities go back to the origin.

Pull-through caching has two costs in this setting. The first viewer of a title in a neighbourhood waits while the edge server fetches it from far away, and that fetch happens at the moment of demand, which for video is the evening peak, when the provider's links to the outside are fullest.

Netflix had something most CDNs do not: a catalogue it controls, and a good idea of what each region will watch tomorrow (the new releases, what was popular today, what is popular among similar viewers). So Open Connect does not wait to be asked. Each night, software in the cloud works out which files every appliance should hold, and the appliances fetch them during a **fill window** in the small hours, when the links are nearly idle and a provider paying for transit at its 95th percentile pays nothing extra for them. In the evening the appliance serves what it already holds. This is called **pre-positioning**, and it trades a prediction problem for most of the miss traffic. The window sets the fill rate: a box that must take in 20 TB of new files in six hours needs 20 × 10¹² × 8 bits / 21,600 s, about 7.4 Gb/s. The prediction is judged by the share of the evening's bytes the box served from its own disks rather than fetched: its hit ratio.

The appliances themselves were built to push as many bytes as possible out of one box. By around 2017 Netflix's engineers were serving about 100 Gb/s from one server, and in 2021 they described a single FreeBSD server sending about 400 Gb/s of encrypted video, by moving the encryption into the operating system's kernel so that file data goes from disk to network card without being copied through the program.[^ktls] At 5 Mb/s a stream, one such box serves about 80,000 viewers.

The control plane stayed in the cloud: sign-in, browsing, recommendations, choosing which appliance serves a viewer, and the nightly fill plans all run in Amazon's regions (lesson 18's services). Only the video bytes come from the edge. It is lesson 6's split between control and data, at the scale of a continent: the small, complicated decisions in one place, and the heavy data flowing by the shortest path.

The last few miles are the least predictable. A home's bandwidth changes from minute to minute as other people in the house start downloads and the neighbourhood's cable fills up. A player that asks for one fixed quality is either wasting a good connection or starving on a poor one.

Modern streaming cuts each video into **segments** a few seconds long, and encodes every segment at several bitrates, an **encoding ladder**; Netflix's fixed ladder in the early 2010s ran from 235 kb/s to 5,800 kb/s for 1080p.[^ladder] A manifest file lists the rungs. The player fetches one segment at a time over plain HTTP, choosing a rung for each, and keeps a **buffer** of segments fetched but not yet shown. Apple's HTTP Live Streaming (2009) and the MPEG-DASH standard (2012) both work this way. Because each segment is an ordinary file, every CDN server, every HTTP cache, is a video server.

blocks.caption: A player's buffer when the bandwidth drops for fifty seconds. The adaptive player picks its rung from how full the buffer is, and never above 80% of the bandwidth it last measured. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: With the bandwidth falling to 2 Mb/s or less, find a player that never stalls, and play it through

blocks.text: The fixed player fetches 5.8 Mb/s segments over a 2 Mb/s link: each four-second segment takes nearly twelve seconds to arrive, the buffer drains, and the picture freezes again and again. The adaptive player drops to a lower rung when the bandwidth falls, keeps its buffer, and climbs back afterwards. Its picture is softer for a minute, and it never stops. Viewers forgive a softer picture far more readily than a frozen one, so players aim to never empty the buffer first and to show the best quality second. Te-Yuan Huang and colleagues at Stanford, working with Netflix, showed in 2014 that choosing the rung mainly from the buffer's level stalled less than choosing it from bandwidth estimates alone. The figure's adaptive player combines the two: it picks a low rung when the buffer is nearly empty and the top one when it is nearly full, but never a rung above 80% of the bandwidth it measured on the last segment.

Netflix built its own CDN because it was a third of the evening's traffic, it had one catalogue it controlled, and video is forgiving of a cache's weaknesses: large files, read whole, rarely changed. Each of those conditions is a reason most companies rent instead. A site with a few hundred terabytes a month buys a CDN by the gigabyte and is done. The break-even is arithmetic. A few hundred terabytes a month averages under 1 Gb/s, nothing to build for. An appliance serving 40 Gb/s at the evening peak saves its provider 40 Gb/s of transit; at an assumed $0.50 per Mb/s a month, that is $20,000 a month, set against the box's price spread over its life, its rack and power, and the staff to run a fleet of them. A site of user uploads, such as YouTube, cannot predict tomorrow's viewing from its catalogue; it relies on pull-through caching for most of its long tail and pre-positions only what it can see coming.

The reasoning carries over to anything with a skewed popularity curve and readers spread across the world: map tiles (the next branch's first lesson), software updates, game downloads, and the static parts of every web page. Find the head of the curve, put it near the readers, and move it when the network is idle.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on moving bytes cheaply
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: An edge cache holding the most popular 10% of a catalogue serves 76% of views. Doubling it to 20% raises that to about 84%. Why so little?
choices: Popularity falls steeply, so each extra title added is watched less than the one before it: the long tail
The cache's disks get slower as they fill, so the extra titles are served too slowly to count as hits
Viewers in a neighbourhood watch the same titles, so a bigger cache only stores more copies of them
items.why: With Zipf popularity the share of views grows only with the logarithm of the cache size. Big gains come from the head of the curve; the tail needs ever more space for each per cent.

items.ask: Why did Netflix fill its edge appliances in the early morning rather than when viewers asked?
choices: Providers allow appliances to fetch only outside their evening peak, under the terms on which they host them
Links are nearly idle then, and transit billed at the peak rate costs nothing extra off-peak, while a miss at 9 p.m. adds to the peak
Fills check each file against the origin, which needs disks that are not busy serving
items.why: Networks are sized and billed for their peak. Moving bytes off-peak is nearly free, and pre-positioned files mean evening views do not cross the provider's outside links at all.

items.ask: A video player's buffer is falling fast and holds only six seconds. What should an adaptive player do with the next segment?
choices: Keep the current bitrate, since changing quality in the middle of a scene is what viewers most dislike
Pause playback until the buffer is full again, then carry on at the bitrate it was using before
Fetch it at a lower bitrate, so it arrives in less time than it plays and the buffer stops draining
items.why: A segment at a bitrate below the bandwidth downloads faster than real time. Viewers mind stalls far more than a softer picture, so protecting the buffer comes first.

items.ask: A service streams 100 million hours of video a day at 5 Mb/s straight from a cloud region at 2 cents a gigabyte. Roughly what does the data cost?
choices: About $36 million a day
About $560,000 a day
About $4.5 million a day
items.why: An hour at 5 Mb/s is 5 × 10⁶ × 3,600 / 8 = 2.25 GB. 100 million hours is 225 million GB, and at $0.02 that is $4.5 million a day. Forgetting to divide bits by 8 gives the $36 million.

items.ask: A site hosts videos uploaded by its users, and most are watched a handful of times. Which way of filling its CDN suits most of its catalogue?
choices: Pull-through caching, since it cannot predict which uploads will be watched where
Pre-positioning every new upload on every edge server overnight, before anyone asks for it
Serving every video from the origin, since caching is of no use to a catalogue with a long tail
items.why: Pre-positioning needs a good prediction and a manageable catalogue. A long tail of uploads fills from the origin on demand, while the head of the curve is still worth caching close to readers.

items.ask: Why is streaming video split into segments of a few seconds, each encoded at several bitrates?
choices: Short files compress better than long ones, so the whole film takes less space on the servers
The player can change quality every few seconds as bandwidth changes, and every segment is an ordinary file any HTTP cache can hold
Each segment can be sent from a different origin, so a film never depends on a single datacentre
items.why: Segments let the player adapt continually, and as plain files over HTTP they flow through CDNs and caches built for the web.

items.ask: Netflix ran sign-in, browsing and recommendations in a cloud region, and served video from appliances inside internet providers. What principle does that split follow?
choices: Keep each customer's data in the country where they live, as data protection rules require
Put the newest software nearest the users, so that bugs show up quickly where they can be seen
Keep the small, complex control decisions in one place, and send the heavy data by the shortest path
items.why: It is the control path and data path split from GFS (lesson 6): decisions are small and change often; bytes are large and travel best directly to the reader.

summary: **Count where the bytes go.** At 5 Mb/s, an hour of video is 2.25 GB, and a hundred million hours a day is hundreds of petabytes.
**Bytes are cheapest when they travel least.** Cloud egress is paid by the gigabyte and transit by the peak rate, while traffic kept inside a provider's network is nearly free.
**A CDN puts copies near readers.** Servers in many networks hold popular content, readers are sent to a near one, and misses go to the origin.
**Popularity is steep, with a long tail.** A cache of a tenth of a catalogue can serve three quarters of the viewing, and each doubling after that gains less.
**Fill when the network is idle.** Pre-positioning tomorrow's likely titles overnight moves the miss traffic out of the evening peak.
**Keep control central and data at the edge.** Netflix ran decisions in the cloud and sent only video bytes from appliances inside providers.
**Adaptive bitrate keeps video playing.** Segments a few seconds long at several bitrates let the player drop quality instead of stalling.
**Build a CDN only when size, a catalogue you control and large files all hold.** Netflix had all three; most services lack one and rent.

sandvine.title: Measuring a third
sandvine.text: Sandvine's reports were built from equipment at many providers, and its figures for Netflix's share of North American peak downstream traffic ran from about 30% in 2011 to the high 30s by the middle of the decade. They are estimates from a sample of networks, not a census.

lewin.title: Danny Lewin
lewin.text: Lewin, Akamai's chief technology officer, was a passenger on American Airlines Flight 11 on 11 September 2001 and was killed when it was flown into the World Trade Center. He was 31.

p95.title: The 95th percentile
p95.text: The provider's traffic rate is sampled every five minutes for a month, the top 5% of samples (about 36 hours) are thrown away, and the highest remaining sample is the rate billed. Short bursts are free; whatever runs every evening is paid for, and whatever runs at 4 a.m. usually is not.

ktls.title: Encryption in the kernel
ktls.text: Serving HTTPS normally means reading file data into the server program, encrypting it there and writing it back to the kernel for the network. With the encryption done inside the kernel, or on the network card itself, the data can go straight from the page cache to the wire, as Kafka's sendfile did in lesson 16.

ladder.title: A ladder per title
ladder.text: In December 2015 Netflix moved from one ladder for everything to a ladder chosen for each title. A cartoon of flat colours looks fine at a far lower bitrate than a grainy war film, so each title got the rungs its own pictures needed, which saved bandwidth on simple titles and raised quality on hard ones.
